title: Add Without Plus or Minus
statement:
You get two signed 32-bit integers a and b. Return a + b.

The catch: you may not use the + or − operators anywhere in your solution, including +=, ++, −= and −−. Build the sum from bitwise operators.

The true sum is guaranteed to fit in a signed 32-bit integer, so the answer is always the ordinary mathematical sum. The checker cannot see which operators you used; keeping to the rule is the point of the exercise.

examples.why: 12 = 1100 and 9 = 1001. XOR alone gives 0101 = 5 because it drops the carry from the shared top bit. The carry (1000 shifted left to 10000 = 16) must be added back: 5 + 16 = 21.
A negative operand. In Python the plain XOR-and-carry loop never ends here: Python ints act as if they had infinitely many sign bits, so the carry keeps walking left forever. A 32-bit mask stops it.
The two 32-bit extremes. 0111…1 and 1000…0 share no 1 bits, so there is no carry, and the result 1111…1 reads as −1 in two's complement.

hints: Add two single bits by hand. Which bitwise operator gives the sum bit, and which gives the carry?

For whole numbers: a ^ b is the sum without carries, and (a & b) << 1 is the carries, already shifted to where they land. Now you need to add those two, which is the same problem again. Why does it end?

Loop until the carry is 0. In JavaScript the 32-bit operators make that happen on their own. In Python, keep both values inside 0xFFFFFFFF and turn a result with bit 31 set back into a negative number at the end.

explain.intuition:
Adding one bit to another: the sum bit is 1 when exactly one input is 1, which is XOR, and a carry appears when both are 1, which is AND. For whole numbers, a ^ b adds every column without carrying and (a & b) << 1 collects every carry, moved one column left to where it lands. Their sum equals a + b. Repeat with those two values until the carry is 0. Each round pushes the lowest possible carry position at least one column left, so in 32 bits there are at most 32 rounds.

JavaScript works out of the box: ^, & and << act on signed 32-bit integers, so a carry out of bit 31 is simply dropped, exactly like hardware. Python is the real lesson. Its ints have no width, and a negative number behaves like an endless run of 1 bits on the left. Add −1 and 1 and the carry crawls left forever. The fix is to simulate a 32-bit register: AND both values with MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF so they become their unsigned 32-bit patterns, and mask the carry each round so it falls off the top. At the end, a value above 0x7FFFFFFF has its sign bit set and stands for a negative number. Convert it with ~(x ^ MASK): x ^ MASK flips the low 32 bits, and ~ flips every bit again, including the infinite ones above, which yields the same bits with the sign extended forever. That equals x − 2³², computed without a minus sign.
steps: While b is not 0: carry = (a & b) << 1, a = a ^ b, b = carry.
TypeScript: return a. The operators already keep everything in signed 32 bits.
Python: first set a &= MASK, b &= MASK, and mask the carry each round: b = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK.
Python: if a ≤ 0x7FFFFFFF return it; otherwise return ~(a ^ MASK) to restore the negative value.
pitfalls: Porting the JavaScript loop to Python unchanged. With a negative operand it never finishes, because the carry never runs out of 1 bits to walk into.
Masking in Python but returning the masked value as is. −4 comes back as 4294967292.
Converting back with a − (1 << 32). It gives the right number but uses the forbidden minus; ~(a ^ MASK) does the same with bit operations.

solutions.title: Ripple-carry, one bit at a time
solutions.idea: Simulate a hardware adder: for each of the 32 positions, the sum bit is a ^ b ^ carry and the next carry is the majority of the three bits.

solutions.title: XOR for the sum, AND for the carry
solutions.idea: a ^ b adds without carries, (a & b) << 1 holds the carries. Repeat until no carry is left. Python needs a 32-bit mask to stop the carry.

followups: How would you subtract a − b with the same tools? (Hint: −b is ~b plus 1.)
If the true sum could overflow, what would each solution return, and what does that tell you about how CPUs add?
